p.src: Now Liu Bei, having twice failed to find Kongming at home, wished to visit him once more. Guan Yu said, “Brother, you have twice gone in person to pay your respects; you have shown him more than enough courtesy. I suspect Zhuge Liang has an empty reputation but no true learning, and therefore avoids you because he dares not meet you. Why are you so utterly captivated by this man?” Liu Bei replied, “That is not so. In former times, Duke Huan of Qi wished to meet the recluse of Dongguo, and only after going back five times did he finally obtain an audience. How much more should I persist when I seek to meet a great worthy?” Zhang Fei said, “Brother, you are mistaken. How could a mere rustic like him deserve to be called a great worthy? This time you need not go, Brother. If he will not come, I shall bind him with a hempen rope and drag him here!” Liu Bei rebuked him: “Have you never heard how King Wen of Zhou paid court to Jiang Ziya? Even King Wen showed such reverence for a worthy man. How can you be so discourteous? You shall stay behind this time. I will go with Yunchang.” Zhang Fei said, “If both my elder brothers are going, how can your younger brother remain behind?” Liu Bei said, “If you come with us, you must not behave discourteously.”

p.src: Zhang Fei gave his word. The three then mounted their horses and led their attendants toward Longzhong. Half a li from the thatched cottage, Liu Bei dismounted and proceeded on foot, whereupon he encountered Zhuge Jun. Liu Bei hastened to salute him and asked, “Is your elder brother at the estate?” Zhuge Jun replied, “He returned only yesterday evening. You will be able to meet him today, General.” With that, he drifted gracefully away. Liu Bei said, “By good fortune, we shall meet the master this time!” Zhang Fei said, “What an ill-mannered fellow! It would have cost him nothing to lead us to the estate. Why did he simply go off on his own?” Liu Bei replied, “He has affairs of his own. How could we compel him?”

p.src: The three reached the front of the estate and knocked at the gate. A young servant opened it and came out to ask their business. Liu Bei said, “May I trouble you, young sir, to announce that Liu Bei has come especially to pay his respects to your master?” The boy replied, “Although the master is at home today, he is taking his midday sleep in the thatched hall and has not yet awakened.” Liu Bei said, “If that is so, do not announce me yet.” He instructed Guan Yu and Zhang Fei to wait at the gate. Liu Bei entered with measured steps and saw the master lying on his back upon a couch in the thatched hall. Liu Bei stood below the steps with hands respectfully clasped.

p.src: A long while passed, but the master did not wake. Guan Yu and Zhang Fei had stood outside for a long time without hearing any movement. When they entered, they saw Liu Bei still waiting on his feet. Zhang Fei flew into a rage and said to Yunchang, “How arrogant this master is! He sees my brother standing in attendance below the steps, yet he lies there grandly, pretending to sleep and refusing to rise! Let me set a fire behind the house and see whether he gets up then!” Yunchang repeatedly restrained and remonstrated with him. Liu Bei again ordered the two men to wait outside the gate. p.src: When Kongming had finished chanting, he turned over and asked the boy, “Have any worldly visitors come?” The boy replied, “Imperial Uncle Liu is here and has been standing outside for a long while.” Kongming rose and said, “Why did you not tell me sooner? Allow me time to change my clothes.” He then withdrew into the rear hall. Only after another long interval did he emerge, properly robed and capped, to receive his guest. Liu Bei saw that Kongming stood eight chi tall, with a face fair as a jade ornament. He wore a silk cap and a cloak of crane down, and possessed the ethereal bearing of an immortal. Liu Bei bowed low and said, “I am a distant scion of the House of Han and an ignorant man from Zhuo Commandery. Long have I heard your great name, Master; it has rung in my ears like thunder. Twice before I came to pay my respects but was denied a meeting. I wrote my humble name upon a note at your writing table; I do not know whether it came to your attention.” Kongming replied, “I am but a rustic of Nanyang, indolent and negligent by nature. That you, General, have repeatedly deigned to visit me fills me with boundless shame.”

p.src: After exchanging courtesies, the two took their seats as host and guest. The boy served tea. When they had finished their tea, Kongming said, “From the meaning of your letter, I could readily see, General, how deeply you care for the people and the realm. Yet I fear that my youth and shallow abilities make me unworthy of the question you have condescended to ask.” Liu Bei said, “Could the words of Sima Decao and Xu Yuanzhi truly have been empty praise? I beg you not to disdain my humble station, but to bend your wisdom to instruct me.” Kongming replied, “Decao and Yuanzhi are eminent gentlemen of this age. I am merely a ploughman. How should I dare discourse upon the affairs of the realm? Those two gentlemen have commended me in error. Why, General, would you cast aside fine jade and seek a common stone?” Liu Bei replied, “When a great man possesses extraordinary talent for ordering the age, how can he grow old in vain among forests and springs? I beg you to keep the common people of the realm in your thoughts, enlighten me in my ignorance, and grant me your instruction.” Kongming smiled and said, “I should like to hear of your ambitions, General.” Liu Bei dismissed the attendants, drew his seat nearer, and said, “The House of Han is collapsing, treacherous ministers have usurped its authority, and I, without measuring my own strength, wish to uphold righteousness throughout the realm. Yet my wisdom and resource are meager, and to this day I have accomplished nothing. If only you would enlighten me in my folly and deliver me from this plight, it would be the greatest of blessings.”

p.src: Kongming said, “Since Dong Zhuo began his rebellion, heroes have risen throughout the realm. Cao Cao’s power was once inferior to Yuan Shao’s, yet he ultimately defeated Shao—not through favorable timing alone, but also through human strategy. Now Cao Cao commands a million men and holds the Son of Heaven in his grasp to issue orders to the lords. He truly cannot be opposed head-on. Sun Quan holds Jiangdong, which his house has ruled for three generations. The land is naturally secure and the people are devoted to him. He may be taken as an ally, but must not be made an object of conquest. Jingzhou is shielded to the north by the Han and Mian rivers, draws all the wealth of the southern seas, connects eastward with Wu and Kuaiji, and opens westward into Ba and Shu. It is a land made for warfare, yet its present lord is incapable of holding it. It is surely Heaven’s gift to you, General. How could you cast it aside? Yizhou is rugged and strongly defended, with fertile plains stretching a thousand li. It is a land endowed by Heaven, and from it Gaozu accomplished his imperial enterprise. Liu Zhang is now benighted and feeble. Though his people are numerous and his realm wealthy, he does not know how to cherish them; men of wisdom and ability long for an enlightened lord. You, General, are a scion of the imperial house; your faith and righteousness are renowned throughout the four seas; you gather heroes around you and thirst for worthy men. If you gain possession of Jingzhou and Yizhou, secure their rugged defenses, make peace with the western tribes, pacify the Yi and Yue peoples in the south, ally outwardly with Sun Quan, and cultivate good government within— then, when the realm undergoes a change, order one great general to lead the forces of Jingzhou toward Wan and Luoyang, while you personally lead the armies of Yizhou out through the Qin Riverlands. Would any of the common people fail to welcome you with baskets of food and vessels of drink? If this is truly done, then the great enterprise may be accomplished and the House of Han restored. This is the strategy I have devised for you, General. I pray you consider it.” When he had finished, he ordered the boy to bring out a scroll map and hang it in the central hall. Pointing to it, he said to Liu Bei, “This is a map of the fifty-four prefectures of Xichuan. If you wish to establish hegemony, concede to Cao Cao in the north the advantage of Heaven’s timing, and to Sun Quan in the south the advantage of the land; you, General, may claim the harmony of the people. First take Jingzhou as your domain, then seize Xichuan as the foundation of your enterprise, thereby forming a balance of three powers. Only then may you seek to gain the Central Plain.”

p.src: Xuande bowed and entreated Kongming, saying, “Though my name is obscure and my virtue slight, I pray that you, sir, will not disdain my humble station, but leave your retreat and come to my aid. I shall respectfully heed your wise instruction.” Kongming replied, “I have long delighted in ploughing and hoeing, and am too indolent to engage with the world. I cannot obey your command.” Xuande wept and said, “If you will not come forth, sir, what is to become of the common people?” When he had finished speaking, tears soaked his sleeves and drenched the whole front of his robe. Seeing the depth of his sincerity, Kongming said, “Since you do not disdain me, General, I am willing to serve you with the faithfulness of a hound or horse.”

Xuande said, “These are no fitting gifts with which to engage a great worthy; they merely express the small measure of Liu Bei’s devotion.” Only then did Kongming accept them. p.src: Xuande and his two companions took leave of Zhuge Jun and returned to Xinye with Kongming. Xuande treated Kongming as his teacher: they ate at the same table, slept on the same couch, and discussed the affairs of the realm together all day long. Kongming said, “Cao Cao has constructed the Black Tortoise Pond in Jizhou to train a naval force. He must intend to invade the lands south of the Yangtze. You should secretly send someone across the river to learn the true state of affairs.” Xuande followed his advice and sent a man to Jiangdong to gather intelligence.

p.src: Now after Sun Ce’s death, Sun Quan held Jiangdong, inherited the foundations laid by his father and elder brother, and recruited worthy men far and wide. He opened a guest lodge at Wuhui and ordered Gu Yong and Zhang Hong to receive visitors from every quarter. Over successive years, one man recommended another. Among them was Kan Ze of Kuaiji, whose courtesy name was Derun; Yan Jun of Pengcheng, whose courtesy name was Mancai; Xue Zong of Pei County, whose courtesy name was Jingwen; Cheng Bing of Runan, whose courtesy name was Deshu; Zhu Huan of Wu Commandery, whose courtesy name was Xiumu; Lu Ji, whose courtesy name was Gongji; Zhang Wen of Wu, whose courtesy name was Huishu; Luo Tong of Kuaiji, whose courtesy name was Gongxu; and Wu Can of Wucheng, whose courtesy name was Kongxiu. All these men came to Jiangdong. Sun Quan treated them with the greatest honor and courtesy. He also obtained several able generals: Lü Meng of Ruyang, whose courtesy name was Ziming; Lu Xun of Wu Commandery, whose courtesy name was Boyan; Xu Sheng of Langya, whose courtesy name was Wenxiang; Pan Zhang of Dong Commandery, whose courtesy name was Wengui; and Ding Feng of Lujiang, whose courtesy name was Chengyuan. These civil and military officers all joined in supporting him. From that time onward, Jiangdong was renowned for its abundance of talented men.

p.src: In the seventh year of Jian’an, after Cao Cao defeated Yuan Shao, he sent an envoy to Jiangdong ordering Sun Quan to send a son to court to attend the imperial entourage. Sun Quan hesitated and could not decide. Lady Wu ordered Zhou Yu, Zhang Zhao, and the others to confer with her in person. Zhang Zhao said, “Cao Cao wishes us to send a son to court because this is his way of keeping the feudal lords under restraint. Yet if we refuse to send him, I fear Cao Cao will raise an army and descend upon Jiangdong, placing us in grave peril.” Zhou Yu said, “General, you have inherited the legacy left by your father and brother and command the people of six commanderies. Your troops are well trained, your provisions abundant, and your officers and soldiers ready to obey. What compulsion is there that you should send a hostage to another man? Once the hostage enters the court, you will have no choice but to ally yourself with the house of Cao; whenever they summon you by command, you will have no choice but to go; and thus you will be controlled by another. It would be better not to send him, but to watch developments at leisure and devise some sound strategy to resist Cao Cao.” Lady Wu said, “Gongjin speaks rightly.” Sun Quan therefore followed his counsel, politely dismissed the envoy, and did not send his son. From that time, Cao Cao conceived the intention of descending upon Jiangnan. But since the north was not yet pacified, he had no leisure to campaign in the south.

p.src: In the eleventh month of the eighth year of Jian’an, Sun Quan led an army against Huang Zu and fought him on the Great River. Huang Zu’s army was defeated. Sun Quan’s general Ling Cao led the advance in a light vessel and fought his way into Xiakou, but was shot dead by an arrow from Huang Zu’s general Gan Ning. Ling Cao’s son Ling Tong, then only fifteen years old, fought desperately to recover his father’s body and bring it back. Seeing that circumstances were unfavorable, Sun Quan withdrew his army and returned to Eastern Wu.

p.src: Now Sun Quan’s younger brother Sun Yi was Administrator of Danyang. Sun Yi was violent by nature and fond of wine, and when drunk he would often flog his soldiers. Gui Lan, the military commander of Danyang, and Dai Yuan, the assistant administrator, had long harbored thoughts of killing Sun Yi. They therefore made a confidant of Sun Yi’s attendant Bian Hong and plotted with him to murder their lord. At that time, all the generals and county magistrates assembled at Danyang. Sun Yi prepared a banquet to entertain them. Sun Yi’s wife, Lady Xu, was beautiful and intelligent, and highly skilled in divination by the Changes; that day she cast a hexagram whose signs were most ominous, and urged Sun Yi not to go out to meet his guests. Sun Yi did not listen, but went ahead with the great gathering.

u.src: Now Sun Quan’s younger brother Sun Yi was Administrator of Danyang.
Sun Yi was violent by nature and fond of wine, and when drunk he would often flog his soldiers.

Gui Lan, the military commander of Danyang, and Dai Yuan, the assistant administrator, had long harbored thoughts of killing Sun Yi. They therefore made a confidant of Sun Yi’s attendant Bian Hong and plotted with him to murder their lord.
At that time, all the generals and county magistrates assembled at Danyang.
Sun Yi prepared a banquet to entertain them.
Sun Yi’s wife, Lady Xu, was beautiful and intelligent, and highly skilled in divination by the Changes;
that day she cast a hexagram whose signs were most ominous, and urged Sun Yi not to go out to meet his guests.
Sun Yi did not listen, but went ahead with the great gathering.

p.src: In the evening, when the feast had ended, Bian Hong followed Sun Yi outside with a sword, drew it at once, and cut him down. Gui Lan and Dai Yuan then laid the blame on Bian Hong and had him beheaded in the marketplace. The two men took advantage of the situation to seize Sun Yi’s household wealth and concubines. Gui Lan, seeing Lady Xu’s beauty, said to her, “I avenged your husband; you must now become mine. If you refuse, you will die.” Lady Xu replied, “My husband has only just died; I cannot bear to yield to you at once. Wait until the last day of the month, when I shall offer sacrifice and put off my mourning garments; after that, it will not be too late for us to marry.”

p.src: Gui Lan agreed. Lady Xu then secretly summoned Sun Gao and Fu Ying, two of Sun Yi’s trusted former officers, into the residence. Weeping, she told them, “While my late husband lived, he often spoke of the loyalty and righteousness of you two gentlemen. Now the two villains Gui and Dai conspired to murder my husband, placed all the blame upon Bian Hong alone, and divided between themselves all our household wealth, servants, and maids. Gui Lan also intends to take me by force; I have falsely consented in order to set his mind at ease. You two generals must send a man with all speed, traveling by night, to inform the Marquis of Wu. Meanwhile, devise a secret plan to destroy the two villains and avenge this wrong and humiliation. Whether I live or die, I shall bear your kindness in my heart!” When she had finished speaking, she bowed twice. Sun Gao and Fu Ying both wept and said, “We have always been grateful for our lord’s gracious treatment. The only reason we did not die with him at once was that we intended to plan his revenge. How could we dare not exert ourselves in carrying out your command, madam?”

p.src: Gui Lan was delighted when he heard of this. That night, Lady Xu sent a maid to invite Gui Lan into the residence. A banquet was laid in the hall, and they drank wine. When he was drunk, Lady Xu invited him into the secret chamber. Delighted, Gui Lan entered in his drunkenness. Lady Xu cried aloud, “Generals Sun and Fu, where are you?” The two men immediately sprang from behind the curtains with swords in hand. Taken completely by surprise, Gui Lan was felled to the ground by one stroke from Fu Ying; Sun Gao struck him once more, killing him on the spot. Lady Xu then sent another invitation asking Dai Yuan to attend the feast. When Dai Yuan entered the residence and reached the hall, he too was killed by Generals Sun and Fu. At the same time, they sent men to put the families of the two villains and the rest of their accomplices to death. Lady Xu then put her mourning garments on again and offered the heads of Gui Lan and Dai Yuan before Sun Yi’s spirit tablet. Within a day, Sun Quan personally led troops to Danyang. Seeing that Lady Xu had already slain the two villains Gui and Dai, he appointed Sun Gao and Fu Ying as Commandants of the Gate and ordered them to guard Danyang, then took Lady Xu back to his own household to be cared for in her old age. p.src: Now the bandits in the hills throughout Eastern Wu had all been pacified. More than seven thousand warships lay upon the Great River. Sun Quan appointed Zhou Yu Grand Commander and placed all the land and naval forces of Jiangdong under his command. In the tenth month of winter, in the twelfth year of Jian'an, Sun Quan's mother, Lady Wu, fell gravely ill. She summoned Zhou Yu and Zhang Zhao and said, “I was born in Wu. Having lost my parents in childhood, I moved with my younger brother Wu Jing to the region of Yue. Later I married into the Sun family and bore four sons. When my eldest son, Ce, was born, I dreamed that the moon entered my breast. Later, when I bore my second son, Quan, I dreamed that the sun entered my breast. A diviner said, ‘She who dreams that the sun and moon enter her breast will surely bear sons destined for greatness.’ Sadly, Ce died young, and now the foundations of Jiangdong have been entrusted to Quan. I pray that you gentlemen will unite in supporting him; then even in death my name shall not perish!” She also charged Sun Quan: “Serve Zibu and Gongjin with the respect due to teachers and mentors, and never treat them carelessly. My younger sister and I both married your father, so she too is your mother. After my death, serve her as you have served me. You must also care tenderly for your younger sister and choose a worthy husband for her.”

p.src: With these words, she passed away. Sun Quan wept bitterly and observed every funeral rite; there is no need to recount the details. When spring came the following year, Sun Quan consulted his officers about attacking Huang Zu. Zhang Zhao said, “A full year of mourning has not yet passed; we must not raise an army.” Zhou Yu said, “Why wait a full year to avenge our wrongs and wipe away our shame?” Sun Quan hesitated, unable to decide. Just then Lü Meng, Commandant of Beiping, came to see him and reported, “While I was guarding the mouth of Longqiu, Gan Ning, one of Huang Zu's officers, suddenly came to surrender. I questioned him closely. Ning's style name is Xingba, and he is a native of Linjiang in Ba Commandery. He is well versed in books and histories, possesses great strength, and delights in the ways of wandering swordsmen. He once gathered desperate fugitives around him and roamed freely across the rivers and lakes. He wore copper bells at his waist, and whenever people heard them, they all fled from his path. He also used brocade from Western Sichuan for his sails and awnings, so people of the time called him the ‘Brocade-Sail Bandit.’ Later, regretting his former misdeeds, he reformed and led his followers to join Liu Biao. When he saw that Liu Biao could accomplish nothing, he intended to join Eastern Wu, but Huang Zu detained him at Xiakou.

p.src: “When Eastern Wu previously defeated Huang Zu, it was through Gan Ning's efforts that Huang Zu escaped back to Xiakou; yet Huang Zu treated him very poorly. Commander Su Fei repeatedly recommended Gan Ning to Huang Zu. Huang Zu said, ‘Ning is nothing but a river pirate. How could he be entrusted with high office?’ Gan Ning therefore bore him a grudge. Su Fei understood his feelings, so he prepared wine, invited Ning to his home, and said, ‘I have recommended you several times, but unfortunately my lord will not employ you. The days and months hasten by, and how brief is human life! You should make plans for your distant future. I shall sponsor you as magistrate of E County, and from there you may decide for yourself whether to stay or depart.’ Thus Gan Ning was able to pass beyond Xiakou. He wished to join Jiangdong, but feared that its people hated him for saving Huang Zu and killing Ling Cao. I explained fully that my lord thirsts for worthy men and bears no old grudges; besides, each man was serving his own master, so what cause was there for hatred? Gan Ning gladly led his followers across the river and has come to see you, my lord. I await Your Lordship's decision.”

p.src: Sun Quan was overjoyed. “Now that I have Xingba,” he said, “Huang Zu is certain to be defeated.” He immediately ordered Lü Meng to bring Gan Ning before him. When the formal greetings were complete, Sun Quan said, “Your coming here, Xingba, greatly pleases me. How could I possibly bear you a grudge? Have no doubts. I ask you to teach me a strategy for defeating Huang Zu.” Gan Ning replied, “The fortunes of the Han decline by the day, and Cao Cao will ultimately usurp the throne. The lands south of Jingzhou are places Cao Cao will certainly contest. Liu Biao lacks foresight, and his sons are foolish and unworthy, incapable of inheriting and preserving his domain. My enlightened lord should plan to seize it early. If you delay, Cao Cao will move first. For now, you should first take Huang Zu. Huang Zu is now old, muddle-headed, and intent only upon profit; he oppresses officials and commoners alike, and all hearts resent him; his weapons and equipment are ill maintained, and his army knows no discipline. If my enlightened lord attacks him, he is certain to fall. Once Huang Zu's army is defeated, advance westward with drums sounding, occupy the passes of Chu, and set your designs upon Ba and Shu; then your hegemony may be secured.”

p.src: Sun Quan said, “These are words precious as gold and jade!” He then appointed Zhou Yu Grand Commander over all the land and naval forces; Lü Meng was made vanguard commander; Dong Xi and Gan Ning were made his deputies; and Sun Quan personally led an army of one hundred thousand to campaign against Huang Zu. Scouts learned of the movement and carried word to Jiangxia. Huang Zu hurriedly assembled his officers for counsel. He appointed Su Fei chief general and Chen Jiu and Deng Long vanguard commanders, then mustered every soldier in Jiangxia to meet the enemy. Chen Jiu and Deng Long each led a squadron of mengchong warships to block the mouth of the Mian. Each vessel carried more than a thousand powerful bows and heavy crossbows, and great cables moored the ships firmly upon the water. When the Eastern Wu troops arrived, drums thundered aboard the mengchong and bows and crossbows discharged together. The soldiers dared not advance and withdrew some miles across the water. Gan Ning said to Dong Xi, “Matters have come to this; we have no choice but to advance.” He selected more than a hundred small boats and placed fifty picked soldiers aboard each: twenty to propel the boat and thirty clad in armor and armed with steel sabers. Defying arrows and stones, they drove straight alongside the mengchong and hacked through the great cables, leaving the warships slewed broadside.

p.src: Gan Ning leaped aboard a mengchong and cut Deng Long down. Chen Jiu abandoned his ship and fled. Seeing this, Lü Meng jumped into a small boat, took up an oar himself, drove straight into the fleet, and set the ships ablaze. As Chen Jiu hastened toward the bank, Lü Meng pursued him with utter disregard for his own life, caught him, and felled him with a saber stroke to the chest. By the time Su Fei led troops to support them from the bank, the Wu army had landed as one, and its onslaught was irresistible. Huang Zu's army was utterly defeated. Su Fei fled wildly, only to encounter the Eastern Wu general Pan Zhang. Their horses met, and after only a few exchanges Pan Zhang captured him alive and took him straight to Sun Quan aboard his ship. Sun Quan ordered his attendants to confine Su Fei in a barred prison cart, intending to execute him together with Huang Zu once the latter had been captured alive; then he urged all three divisions onward to assault Xiakou day and night without respite.
